cards.title: Crack spread
lines: What a refiner earns for 'cracking' crude into products.
Product price minus crude price, both in $/bbl.
Gasoline at $2.50/gal = $105/bbl. Crude at $80 → crack = $25/bbl.
Wide cracks → refiners run hard → more crude demand.

question.prompt: ULSD is $3.00/gal and Brent is $90. What's the diesel crack?

cards.title: 3-2-1 crack
lines: A rough US refinery margin: 3 bbl of crude → 2 gasoline + 1 diesel.
(2×RBOB + 1×ULSD − 3×WTI) ÷ 3, all in $/bbl.
It roughly matches a typical Gulf Coast refinery's output.
Traders use it to hedge or bet on refining margins.

question.prompt: In a 3-2-1, which product gets double weight?
question.explain: Two barrels of gasoline for each barrel of diesel. US refineries are gasoline-heavy.

cards.title: Backwardation
lines: Prompt oil costs MORE than oil for later delivery.
Example: Dec Brent $85, Jun Brent $80.
It means the market is tight. People pay up to have barrels now.
Storage makes no money, so tanks get drained.

question.prompt: Inventories are drawing fast. What curve shape do you expect?
question.explain: Scarce prompt barrels put a premium on 'now', so the front trades over the back.

cards.title: Contango
lines: Prompt oil costs LESS than oil for later delivery.
Example: Dec WTI $70, Jun WTI $74.
That means a glut. Buy now, store, sell forward, and keep the spread.
Deep contango = storage filling up.

question.prompt: Front WTI $60, 6-month-out $63, storage costs $0.30/bbl/month. Profitable carry?
question.explain: $3 spread − 6 × $0.30 storage = $1.20/bbl profit (before financing). That's cash-and-carry.

cards.title: Calendar spread
lines: The price difference between two delivery months of the same contract.
Often quoted M1−M2 (front minus second month).
Positive = backwardation. Negative = contango.
The purest read on near-term supply and demand.

question.prompt: Brent Dec $82.40, Jan $81.90. The Dec/Jan spread is…
question.explain: Front minus next: 82.40 − 81.90 = +0.50, so the front is premium (backwardation).

cards.title: Storage build vs draw
lines: Each Wednesday the EIA reports weekly US inventory changes.
Build = stocks rose (usually bearish). Draw = stocks fell (usually bullish).
What matters is the number vs EXPECTATIONS, not the raw number.
And why: imports, exports or refinery runs.

question.prompt: Consensus: 3M bbl draw. EIA prints a 1M draw. First reaction?
question.explain: Markets trade the surprise. A 1M draw vs 3M expected is effectively a 2M bearish miss.

cards.source: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report, released Wednesdays 10:30 ET.

cards.title: API vs EIA
lines: API (industry group) publishes estimates Tuesday at 4:30pm ET.
EIA (government) publishes official data Wednesday 10:30am ET.
API often sets up the trade, and EIA confirms or reverses it.
Holiday weeks shift both by a day.

question.prompt: Which report is the official US government data?
question.explain: API is a private survey; the EIA's Weekly Petroleum Status Report is the official number.

cards.source: API Weekly Statistical Bulletin; EIA WPSR.

cards.title: Cushing, Oklahoma
lines: The delivery point for NYMEX WTI futures.
A tank-farm hub with roughly 75-80M bbl of working capacity.
Cushing stocks drive WTI's front spreads.
Near 'tank bottoms' → backwardation. Near full → super-contango.

question.prompt: Why did WTI go negative but Brent didn't in April 2020?
choices: WTI delivers physically at landlocked Cushing, which was filling
question.explain: Brent is seaborne and cash-settled against a forward market, so it can flow to ships. May WTI holders had to take barrels at a nearly full inland hub.

cards.source: EIA Cushing working storage capacity reports.

cards.title: Shut-ins
lines: Production deliberately stopped: storms, outages, low prices or politics.
Gulf of Mexico hurricanes are the classic case: platforms evacuate.
Shut-ins are temporary, and output returns when the cause clears.
Watch the restart timeline, not just the size of the outage.

question.prompt: A hurricane shuts 1.5 mb/d of Gulf crude AND 2 mb/d of refining. Crude price impact?
choices: Could be flat or bearish: demand lost exceeds supply lost
question.explain: Refineries are the crude buyers. If more refining shuts than production, crude backs up (see Harvey 2017).

cards.source: BSEE Gulf of Mexico shut-in statistics.

cards.title: Freight rates
lines: The cost to ship oil by tanker, quoted in Worldscale points or $/tonne.
VLCC (2M bbl) on the Gulf→China route (TD3C) is the crude benchmark.
High freight widens price gaps between regions.
War, sanctions and rerouting (e.g. avoiding the Red Sea) push freight up.

question.prompt: Freight from the US Gulf to Asia doubles. US crude (WTI) vs Brent likely…
choices: Widens: WTI must discount to still export
question.explain: US barrels have to cover the higher shipping cost to compete abroad, so WTI weakens relative to Brent.

cards.title: Basis
lines: The price of a physical barrel at a location vs the benchmark futures.
Example: Midland WTI at +$1.00 to Cushing; Mars at −$2.50 to WTI.
It reflects local supply, pipeline space and quality.
Futures can be calm while basis blows out.

question.prompt: A Permian pipeline goes down. What happens to Midland basis vs Cushing?
question.explain: Barrels get trapped near Midland, so local buyers can pay less vs Cushing.

cards.title: Brent−WTI spread
lines: Brent = seaborne North Sea benchmark. WTI = US inland (Cushing).
The spread is mostly logistics: the cost to move US crude to the water and across the ocean.
It's normally ~$3-6 in Brent's favour since the 2015 export-ban repeal.
US export capacity sets the floor.

question.prompt: US Gulf export terminals are congested. Brent−WTI tends to…
question.explain: If US barrels can't get out, they back up at home and WTI discounts more to Brent.

cards.title: Sweet vs sour
lines: Sweet = low sulfur (<0.5%). Sour = high sulfur.
Sour crude needs more processing to remove the sulfur.
So sour normally trades at a discount to sweet.
OPEC cuts usually remove sour barrels, which narrows that discount.

question.prompt: OPEC+ cuts 1 mb/d of medium-sour supply. The sweet-sour spread…
question.explain: Less sour supply means sour barrels get bid up relative to sweet.

cards.title: API gravity
lines: A measure of how light a crude is. Higher = lighter.
WTI ~40°. Brent ~38°. Heavy Canadian ~20°.
Light crude yields more gasoline and naphtha.
Heavy crude yields more residual fuel and needs complex refineries.

question.prompt: Which crude yields more gasoline per barrel?
question.explain: Lighter (higher API) crude has more light ends: gasoline and naphtha.

cards.title: Summer vs winter gasoline
lines: RVP measures how easily gasoline evaporates.
Summer gasoline must have low RVP (less smog), which costs more to make.
Winter-grade allows cheap butane to be blended in.
So RBOB futures drop at the summer-to-winter grade roll.

question.prompt: Why does the RBOB crack usually fall in September?
choices: Switch to cheaper winter-grade plus lower driving demand
question.explain: Winter spec lets refiners blend more cheap butane, and demand fades after Labor Day.

cards.source: EPA RVP regulations; NYMEX RBOB contract specs.

cards.title: Refinery utilization
lines: The share of refining capacity running. The US is typically 85-95%.
It's in the weekly EIA report.
High runs = strong crude demand and more product supply.
Spring and autumn 'turnarounds' (maintenance) cut runs.

question.prompt: Refinery runs drop from 92% to 80% for maintenance. Crude stocks likely…
question.explain: Fewer refineries buying crude → crude piles up in tanks while product stocks fall.

cards.title: Strategic Petroleum Reserve
lines: The US government's emergency crude stockpile in Gulf Coast salt caverns.
Releases add supply (bearish), and refills add demand (bullish).
2022 saw a record 180M bbl release after the invasion of Ukraine.
The EIA reports commercial stocks separately from the SPR.

question.prompt: The DOE announces a 30M bbl SPR purchase over 6 months. Effect?
question.explain: Buying for the SPR takes barrels off the market: ~165 kb/d here, small but supportive.

cards.source: US DOE Office of Petroleum Reserves.

cards.title: OPEC+ spare capacity
lines: Output that can be brought online within ~30-90 days and held there.
Mostly in Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
Low spare capacity = less buffer, so outages spike prices more.
It's the market's shock absorber.

question.prompt: Spare capacity is ~1 mb/d and a 2 mb/d outage hits. Expect…
choices: A big price spike: no buffer
question.explain: With not enough spare capacity to replace the loss, price has to rise to cut demand instead.

cards.source: IEA Oil Market Report; EIA STEO.

cards.title: Floating storage
lines: Using tankers as tanks: loading crude and parking them at sea.
It only pays when contango beats tanker charter cost.
A sign of a serious glut, as seen in 2009 and 2020.
When contango narrows, ships discharge and add supply.

question.prompt: Contango is $1/bbl/month. A VLCC (2M bbl) costs $60k/day. Floating storage pays?
question.explain: $1 × 2M bbl = $2M per month of carry vs $60k × 30 = $1.8M charter, a thin profit before finance and insurance.

cards.title: Roll yield
lines: Long futures positions must 'roll': sell the expiring month, buy the next.
In backwardation you sell high and buy lower, a positive roll.
In contango you sell low and buy higher, so you lose on every roll.
That's why oil ETFs bled in 2020.

question.prompt: You hold long oil via futures in steep contango. Spot price unchanged for a year. Your P&L?
question.explain: Every roll buys the more expensive next month, which then converges down toward spot.

cards.title: Futures expiry & physical delivery
lines: NYMEX WTI expires 3 business days before the 25th of the prior month.
Holders at expiry must make or take physical delivery.
Most speculators roll or close out days before.
Expiry days can squeeze if prompt supply is short.

question.prompt: Why do ULSD and WTI sometimes spike or crash on expiry day?
choices: Positions must match physical supply at the delivery point
question.explain: On expiry, paper must turn into barrels or gallons. If local supply is tight or full, price does the clearing.

cards.title: Diesel vs gasoline
lines: Diesel (ULSD, heating oil) is driven by trucking, farming, industry and heating.
Gasoline is driven by consumers driving, and peaks in summer.
Diesel cracks often peak in winter, gasoline cracks in spring and summer.
Europe is short diesel; the US is long gasoline capacity.

question.prompt: A cold winter in the US Northeast most directly lifts…
question.explain: NYMEX 'HO' was literally heating oil, and the Northeast still burns distillate for heat.

cards.title: Netback
lines: What a producer actually receives at the wellhead or port.
Netback = delivered price − freight − fees − quality adjustments.
Traders compare netbacks to pick the best market for a cargo.
Arbitrage flows go where netbacks are highest.

question.prompt: Cargo sells for $84 delivered in Asia, freight $3.50, fees $0.50. Netback?
question.explain: $84 − $3.50 − $0.50 = $80/bbl back at origin.

cards.title: Geopolitical risk premium
lines: Extra price added for supply that MIGHT be lost, not that is lost.
It builds into threats and fades when barrels keep flowing.
'Buy the rumor, sell the fact' is common in oil.
Watch actual flows: tanker tracking and exports.

question.prompt: A feared attack happens but oil infrastructure is untouched. Typical reaction?
choices: Price falls as the premium unwinds
question.explain: The worst case didn't happen, so the insurance priced in gets sold (Oct 2024, Jun 2025).

cards.title: Strait of Hormuz
lines: A narrow channel between Iran and Oman.
About 20 mb/d (~20% of world oil use) passes through.
Only limited pipeline bypasses exist (Saudi East-West, UAE Habshan-Fujairah).
It's the single biggest chokepoint risk in oil.

question.prompt: Roughly what share of global oil consumption transits Hormuz?
question.explain: EIA estimates ~20 mb/d, about one-fifth of global consumption.
